Definition 5.13 (SHSP) 
The  symmetric  HSP  (SHSP) is  the  hidden  subgroup  problem for  the  symmetric  group  Sn. An  efficient algorithm for the symmetric HSP has a complexity poly(n). ◇ 
By Cayley's theorem, every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of S∣G ∣. Hence to find a subgroup H  of G, one can apply a SHSP to the corresponding subgroup of S∣G ∣. However, an efficient algorithm for S∣G ∣ would be poly(∣G∣) while an efficient algorithm for G needs to be poly(log(∣G∣)). 
A more  exciting  application  is that an  efficient algorithm for SHSP would  give  a  solution  to  the  graph isomorphism problem, which has remained unsolved for many decades. We recall: 
Definition 5.14 (Graph isomorphism and automorphism problems) 
Let (V1, E1) and (V2, E2) be two (undirected) graphs. They are said to be isomorphic iff there is a bijection φ : V1 → V2  such  that  for  any  two  vertices  a, b ∈ V1  we  have  {a, b} ∈ E1  iff  {φ(a), φ(b)} ∈ E2.  The  graph 
isomorphism problem is to determine whether two such graphs are isomorphic, in time polynomial in the size of the input parameters (the number of vertices for example). The graph automorphism problem is to determine whether a graph has a non-trivial automorphism (i.e. there exists a φ ≠ Id which is a permutation of the vertices of the graph). ◇ 
Figure 5.4 
The figure 5.4 shows an example of three isomorphic graphs. Clearly, the automorphisms are given by the bijections fixing the vertex of degree 4. 
Notice that the definition above is the decisional version of the graph isomorphism problem. It turns out that finding an explicit isomorphism or counting the number of isomorphism has the same complexity, so we can restrict ourselves to the decisional version. This version is clearly in the class NP, but it is known neither to be NP-complete  nor  to  belong  to  the  class  P.  Many  problems  are  computationally  equivalent  to  the  graph isomorphism problem. For instance, it is the case of the graph automorphism problem, to the weaker version with connected graphs or to the stronger version with directed graphs. See, [Köb1993] for details. 
Let's consider first the reduction of the graph automorphism problem to SHSP. Let (V , E) be a graph and 
38
define H  to  be the set of its automorphisms. Obviously, the identity is an automorphism, the inverse of an automorphism is an  automorphism and  the  composition  of two  automorphisms is again  an  automorphism. Hence H  is a subgroup of the permutations of V  that can itself be viewed as Sn for n = ∣V ∣. We define the oracle f  to be the function that send φ ∈ Sn  to f (φ) = (φ(V ), φ(E)). As indicated in [Lom2004], f  can be computed efficiently. Suppose for instance that we have fixed an enumeration {0, ⋯, n − 1}  of the vertices V  and we represent the graph (V , E) by an ordered list of pairs (a, b) where a ≤ b ∈ V  and {a, b} ∈ E. Given (V , E), we can compute (φ(V ), φ(E)) efficiently by replacing each (a, b) by (φ(a), φ(b)) and then applying classical sorting algorithms on the whole structure. 
Finally, we have H  a subgroup of Sn  and clearly ∀ φ1, φ2 ∈ Sn, f (φ1) = f (φ2) ⇔ φ1H = φ2H . So an efficient 
algorithm for DHSP gives a poly(n) algorithm for determining H . Actually, we only need a weaker version of DHSP where we want to determine whether H  is non-trivial i.e. the graph has a non-trivial automorphism. 
When the two graphs (V1, E1) and (V2, E2) are rigid i.e. do not have a non-trivial automorphism, there exists a reduction from the graph isomorphism problem to a somewhat simpler version of HSP. First, if the graphs do not have the same number of vertices, then they are clearly not isomorphic and we are done. So let n be their 
common number of vertices. It is easy to check whether each graph is connected in time O(n 2 ). Again, if one is

If both are not connected, then their complement graphs are connected  and  using  these  complement  graphs  instead  changes  neither  the  answer  to  the  graph automorphism nor the rigidity of the graphs. Attempts  to  solve  SHSP, even  the  restricted  versions have  not reached  any success so  far. The  first question is whether the classical Fourier Sampling method is helpful. Some negative results were proved for the  weak  Fourier  Sampling  [GriSchVaz2000]  [HalRusTa-2000],  extended  to  strong  Fourier  Sampling [MooRusSch2005] and finally to an arbitrary POVM over many entangled coset states [HalRoeSen2005]. More precisely,  the  last  result  shows  that  we  need  to  perform measurement on  at  least  Ω(log(∣Sn∣)) = Ω(nlog n) 
entangled states at once. 
One model for using such an entanglement is Kuperberg's algorithm for DHSP. It can be interpreted as a repetition of combine-and-measure operations on representation state (i.e. given representation states ρi  and 
ρj, apply measurement on  their  tensor product ρi ⊗ ρj  to  get a  new representation  state) until  we  reach  a representation  from which  one  can  extract useful  information  on  the  hidden  subgroup. [MooRusSni2006], proved however that such an algorithm can not succeed for the symmetric group unless it takes ⅇΩ( n√ )  time. 
This  does  not give  any  meaningful  improvement over  the  best known  classical  algorithms: ⅇO( n log n√ )  for 
general graphs [BabLuk1983] or ⅇ O(n 
1 3 log 2 n) for strongly regular graph [Spi1996]. 
Despite intensive study, no quantum algorithm for SHSP are known. It is worth noting that the structure of the symmetric group is very complex (Sn  contains all the groups of order n as subgroups) and is likely to be much more difficult to solve. It is possible that a straightforward method (i.e. performing coset sampling over the Sn  or Sn ≀ ℤ2) is not appropriate and we should rather distinguish many particular or reduced cases as in the classical algorithms mentioned above, which rely on classification of finite simple groups. Solving HSP for other groups  will  provide  us  more  techniques  and  probably  help  us  to  find  a  general  method.  For  example, O'Nan–Scott theorem gives the form of the maximal subgroups of Sn  and we could use the "maximal subgroup reduction" method given in the next section.

6.1. General approach to the Hidden Subgroup Problem 
In this section, we recall  the two fundamental theorems of group theory describing all  finite groups. We show how they can be used to solve the general HSP under certain conditions. We study the special cases of dedekindian, dihedral and symmetric groups in that framework. 
A group G  is said to be simple, if it contains no other normal subgroups than {1}  and G. Finite simple groups are the "building blocks" for all  finite groups and their classification are given by a theorem of group theory. More precisely, the theorem states that the possibilities for a finite simple group are: 
Cyclic groups ℤp for p prime. Alternating groups An for n ≥ 5. Simple groups of Lie type. 26 sporadic simple groups.

authors of [DamHalIp2002] solved the shifted Legendre symbol problem as well as other related hidden shift problems. They indicate that they can break certain cryptosystems by a reduction to the shifted Legendre symbol problem. They say that these cryptosystems can also be broken by Shor’s algorithm, but the two attacks on the cryptosystems appear to use completely different ideas. Hence this shifted Legendre symbol problem shows another relation between cryptosystems and HSP: it can be reduced to the HSP over G = Dp  (under certain assumptions) and as we will see in the next section it can also be reduced to a HSP over G = ℤp ≀ ℤ2. 
Recall  that  in  Grover's  algorithm  we  have  N  elements  indexed  from  0  to  N − 1,  an  oracle  φ : 
{0, …, N − 1} → {0, 1} taking the value 1 for M ≤ N 2  elements and we want to find one of these elements. Here, 
we  take  M = 1  and  denote  j0  the  element that satisfies  φ( j0) = 1.  Lomonaco  and  Kauffman  proposed  a comparaison between this case and Shor's algorithm [LomKau2006]. They described Shor's algorithm as an infinite HSP over ℤ with a subgroup pℤ hidden by an oracle f . They defined a "push" method, used to reduce 
the problem to some HSP over ℤq  (for some integer q) and a new oracle f .̃ Next, they considered the HSP over SN  with hidden subgroup H = Stabj0  of permutations stabilizing j0. They used the subgroup Stab0 and their 
"push" method  to  get a  new  problem where  the  oracle  f ̃ = φ  is  just Grover's  oracle. However, from the definition of a "push" given of their paper, it is not obvious that their algorithm is applyable since we are loosing the group structure. They say that the definitions of the "push" and Fourier Sampling can be generalized but still the  algorithm fails to  provide  a  solution  [Lom2010] . Anyway, Grover's algorithm can  be  interpreted  as an efficient HSP algorithm for otherwise we would have an exponential  speedup instead of the known optimal quadratic speedup [Zal1997]. Here, we are working over G = SN  and an efficient algorithm is expected to be polynomial in N log N . With the promise H = Stabj0 , we only need to find the j satisfying f (σj) = f (Id) where we 
use the cycle  σj = (0,1, …, j − 1, j + 1, …, N − 1)  moving all  elements but j. This can be done in  O(N)  time classically (brute-force search) or even in O( N√ ) time quantumly (Grover's algorithm) and thus the HSP in that case  is  efficiently  solvable.  This  was  actually  noted  in  [DenMooRus2008],  where  efficient  algorithms  are provided for 1-point stabilizer subgroups of SL(2, q), PGL(2, q), PSL(2, q). Interestingly, the big picture of their algorithm is similar to the "push" method above: rather than working over the whole group, they reduce the sampling to a particular 1-point stabilizer for which they can apply the non-abelian Fourier Sampling. Note that the  size  (or  number of 1-point stabilizers)  of these  three  groups is  polynomial  in  q  and  the  efficient HSP algorithm polynomial in log q. Thus, the following open question: can we interpret these algorithms as concrete search problems with an exponentially fast solution? 
6.4. Variants and Extensions 
In this section, we present various problems related to the Hidden Subgroup Problem. Indeed, there have been several proposals to interpret the efficient algorithms of the first part of this report, other than the abelian HSP. New problems have  been  defined  and  solved  for  some particular  cases. These  problems are  often related  to  HSP and their study has sometimes lead to  solutions to  instances of HSP. More  generally, it is expected that these problems will also provide new quantum algorithms exponentially faster than the classical ones. 
One extension is to allow G to be an infinite group: it was actually already the case for the original Shor's algorithm which reduces the HSP over the infinite group G = ℤ to the HSP over some cyclic group ℤq, for some q large enough. In general, the abelian HSP algorithm works for any finitely generated abelian group such that 
G = ℤn. In order to solve various problem, Hallgren had to introduce HSP over ℝ and ℝr [Hal2002], [Hal2005]. The  HSP he  considered  is  finding  a  hidden  subgroup  H = ⟨τ⟩  of ℝ  generated  by an  irrational  τ  (or  said 
49
otherwise, determining an irrational period τ  of a function f ) as well as finding a hidden lattice H  of ℝr. In both cases, the rough idea is to construct a computable discretized version of the oracle f  and show that we can approximate generators for H . 
Other extensions to HSP have been proposed in  three different papers, but they do not seem to have subsequently been studied. One proposal is the Hidden Subhypergroup Problem [AmiKalRoo2006] where the group G is generalized to an hypergroup i.e. the product of two elements is a subset of G rather than a single element.  A  second  proposal  is  the  Hidden  Symmetries  Problem  [SchUnr2003]  where  we  generalize  the condition  that  f  is  constant  on  each  left  coset  to  a  more  general  property  ∀ x ∈ G, V ( f (x), f (U (x))).  For example, saying that f  hides H  is simply taking V  to be the equality and U (x) = xH . The third proposal is the Hidden  Covering  Space  Problem  [OsbSev2004] which  generalizes  the  version  of  HSP given  as  a  coset sampling black-box. This proposal involves topological spaces and is a bit more complicated to define. We will just say that we consider Cayley graph of groups endowed with their natural topology. 
A variation that has been extensively studied is the Hidden Shift Problem. In this problem, we have two injective functions f0, f1  on G satisfying ∀ x ∈ G, f1(x) = f0(x + s) for some s ∈ G. The purpose is to determine 
the hidden shift s. The problem was solved for many cases, including smoothly solvable groups [FriEtAl2002], bent functions [Röt2008], functions close to a quadratic [Röt2009], Legendre symbol [DamHalIp2002] as well as more  general  multiplicative  characters on  finite  fields and  on  ideals  ℤ 
n ℤ  [DamHalIp2002]. When  G  is abelian, the problem is equivalent to HSP over the generalized dihedral group G⋊ℤN . In particular, for G = ℤN 
the problem is equivalent to DHSP. A decision version is considered in [ChiWoc2005]: either a shift s exists or the images of f0, f1  are disjoint. We are asked to determine in which case we are. A solution to this decision 
version for the symmetric group G = Sn  would provide an efficient algorithm for the rigid graph isomorphism problem. A Generalized Hidden Shift Problem is considered in [ChiDam2005] and solve for the cyclic group G = ℤN  under  certain  conditions.  The  generalization  consists  in  having  M  injective  functions  f0, …, fM − 1 
satisfying ∀ x ∈ G, fi(x) = f0(x + is). Note that the generalized hidden shift problem reduces to HSP over the 
wreath  product  G ≀ ℤM  [FenZha2006].  Hence,  the  two  solutions  to  the  hidden  shift  problem from Rötteler 
mentioned above are particular case of G = ℤ2 n  which is solved from the efficient algorithm he obtained with 
Beth [RötBet1998]. When the functions f0, f1  are  not injective, the set of elements s ∈ G  satisfying the shift 
equality can be proved to be a coset of some subgroup H  [DamHalIp2002]. Finding this set is then called the Hidden  Coset  Problem.  It  turns  out  that  this  problem  is  actually  polynomial-time  equivalent  to  HSP [FenZha2006]. If H  is normal, we can work in the quotient group G H  and reduce the problem to the hidden shift problem [Ip2002], [DamHalIp2002]. 
To solve some HSP instances, Friedl et al. [FriEtAl2002] used several HSP-related problems. In addition to the Hidden Shift Problem discussed above (which is called hidden translation in their paper), they introduced the Hidden Stabilizer Problem, Orbit Coset Problem, and Orbit Superposition Problem. For the first one, we have a group G acting on a set of pairwise orthogonal quantum states. Given such a state we are asked to find its stabilizer subgroup. The second one is a generalization: given two states ∣Ψ0⟩ and ∣Ψ1⟩ we have to answer whether the intersection of their orbits is empty or find an element g ∈ G  sending ∣Ψ0⟩ to ∣Ψ1⟩ as well  as the stabilizer  subgroup  of ∣Ψ1⟩. One  interesting  feature  of Orbit Coset Problem on  a  group  G  is  the  following self-reductibility property: if N  is a solvable normal subgroup of G, then the problem reduces to the Orbit Coset Problem on G N  and on subgroups of N. Notice that such a property would be really appreciated for HSP to design an algorithm similar to the one of figure 6.2. Finally, the Orbit Superposition Problem asks to create the 
50
uniform superposition over the orbit of a given state ∣Ψ ⟩. For solvable groups, it reduces to Orbit Coset Problem. Again, in  [FenZha2006] it is proved that Orbit Coset is polynomial-time equivalent to  the Hidden Subgroup Problem when we allow the oracle f  to be a quantum function. 
As many other problems, decision and search versions of HSP have also been imagined. [FenZha2006] defines HSPD  to  be  the  problem of deciding  whether H  is trivial  and  HSPS  to  be  the  problem of findind  a nontrivial  element of H , if there is one. As we have previously seen, this is of particular importance for the dihedral and symmetric HSP. In the paper, they give a reduction of HSP to HSPD for the dihedral group (under certain conditions) and a polynomial-time equivalence between HSPS  and HSPD  for permutation groups. The latter equivalence suggests that the problem is hard, since we have this property for problems considered to be difficult such that NP-complete or graph isomorphism. Another proposal for a decision version of HSP is the Hidden Subgroup Test Function where we are given G, H , as well as a function f  on G and want to decide whether the function hides the subgroup H . In [AblVas2009], the function f  is encoded as a particular "input sequence". Similarly in [FriEtAl2002bis], the Large Period Problem is studied: we are given G, a subgroup K and a function f . We want to decide whether K  is a proper superset of some subgroup H ⊆ G hidden by f . The problem is solved for abelian subgroups. The paper also defines the Common Coset Range Problem: given H ⊆ G and two functions f0, f1 on G do we have the equality ∀ x ∈ G, f1(xH ) = f0(xH )? Again, the problem is solved for some particular cases. 
Let's consider now the case of the abelian HSP dealing with the vector space G = Fq m over the finite field Fq 
, which is studied in [ChiSchVaz2007]. Any subgroup H  is a linear subspace of G and cosets g + H  are parallel 
affine subspaces. Thus in  the abelian HSP over Fq m  we have an oracle constant on each affine subspace, 
taking  distinct values  on  different ones  and  want to  find  a  subspace  H .  If  H  is  a  hyperplane, there  are 
coefficients qi ∈ Fq  such that the linear polynomial P(x) = ∑ i = 0 
m qi xi satisfies H = KerP. Moreover, P  is constant 
on each coset and takes distinct values on different ones. Thus the oracle can be written f (x) = π(P(x)) for some fixed unknown permutation π  of Fq. The Hidden Polynomial Problem is to determine the polynomial P whose degree is still bounded, but we now allow this degree to be greater than 1. Similarly to the case of the hyperplane H , we assume that the constant term is P(0) = 0, for otherwise that term can not be determined, since  π  is  arbitrary. The  problem can  also  be  viewed  as finding  the  hidden  hypersurface  defined  by  the equation P(x) = 0 and the cosets are replaced by level  hypersurfaces (defined by equations P(x) = k). One special case is when the polynomial is of the form P(x) = xm − Q(x1, …, xm− 1) i.e. the hidden hypersurface is defined by the parametric equation xm = Q(x1, …, xm− 1). In that case, the level hypersurfaces are just obtained by  translating  along  the  xm-axis.  This  problem,  called  Hidden  Polynomial  Function  Graph  Problem  is considered in [DecWoc2007], [DecDraWoc2007] and solved for quadratic and cubic polynomial Q. 
The authors of [ChiSchVaz2007] also consider other hidden structure problems on G = Fq m. They define 
the Hidden Radius Problem: determine an unknown radius r given a blackbox that outputs superposition over the points of a sphere of radius r whose center is chosen uniformly at random. Similarly they define the Hidden Flat of Center: determine a flat given a blackbox that outputs superposition over unit sphere whose center is chosen uniformly at random in the hidden flat. They give a partial solution to the former and a complete solution to the latter. Other algorithms of this kind are given in [Mon2008] for the group G = {0, 1}n. All these problems are included in the more general category of Hidden Shifted Subset Problems. We have a group G, a subset of elements S  and a subset of shifts T  the black box outputs uniform superposition of element over the set S + t for 
51
a t ∈ T  chosen uniformly at random. The purpose is to determine some property of S  or T . To compare their power with the one of a classical computer, we would like an approach similar to HSP where we just have an oracle  f  whose  preimages are  the  possible  superpositions output by the  black box. This  does not seem possible in the general case, since the superpositions considered may intersect but some workarounds are used for the particular problems mentioned above. 
52
7. Conclusion 
In  this  report  we  have  studied  the  Hidden  Subgroup  Problem, whose  solution  for  various  groups  is expected to provide new efficient quantum algorithms. In a first part, we have reviewed the classical efficient Quantum algorithms of Simon and Shor and identified their main features. We have introduced the Hidden Subgroup Problem and showed how the previous algorithms can be defined in that framework. 
In a second part, we have been interested in the standard method based on coset sampling. We have presented the well-known solution to the abelian case which includes the algorithms seen in the first part. We have  described  precisely  a  natural  extension  to  the  non-abelian  case,  by  defining  a  Quantum  Fourier Transform over finite  groups as well  as Weak/Strong Fourier Sampling. We have shown that Weak Fourier Sampling  is able  to  find  normal  hidden subgroups and thus provides a  solution  to  HSP over dedekindian groups.  We  have  mentioned  some  extensions  when  the  group  is,  in  some  sense,  not  too  far  from  a dedekindian group. However, the Weak Fourier Sampling can not distinguish conjugate groups and thus it is not applyable to an arbitrary group. 
In a third part, we have turned our attention to the dihedral and symmetric hidden subgroup problems. We have given a complete presentation of the structure of the dihedral  group and recalled the reduction of the dihedral HSP to the search of a hidden slope d . We have presented Kupenberg's subexponential algorithm to find this slope and mentioned the results about the optimal measurement for dihedral coset sampling. We have studied Regev's algorithm for the uniqueSVP and noticed that it can be modified to work for some generalized dihedral groups and "recursive" coset sampling. We have also shown that the approximation factor obtained for the  uniqueSVP is  strongly  related  to  the  degree  of the  polynomial  bounding  the  complexity  of the  coset sampling  algorithm used.  Finally,  we  have  presented  the  classical  reduction  from graph  isomorphism to symmetric hidden subgroup problems but have also recalled the negative results on the symmetric group: we need at least a linear number of entangled coset states at once but using an algorithm similar to Kupenberg's one does not help. 
In the fourth and last part, we have considered the general HSP. We have suggested a general approach to the hidden subgroup problem based on the mathematical description of finite groups. We have shown that we could reduce the general case to a solution over simple groups and construction of some efficient oracles. These two points are precisely where we are stuck on for dihedral and symmetric groups. However, several efficient algorithms have been discovered for other non-abelian groups. We have given an overview of these solutions which are essentially with respect to "almost abelian" groups in some sense or the other. We have described some efficient algorithms with concrete application, including applications in cryptography, which are related to the hidden subgroup problem. Finally, we have mentioned variants and extensions to the HSP which have been solved for some particular cases and are expected to yield new efficient quantum algorithms. 
As a conclusion, we have provided a good overview of the hidden subgroup problem going from its origin to the state of the art as of 2010. We have also brought some contributions to the topic. While the general problem still  remains difficult, we hope that our work will  help people to have a better understanding of the subject and guide them toward some research directions.

Appendix E: Table of Lattice-based Cryptosystems 
In this section, we sum up in a table the overview of lattice-based cryptosystems given in [MicReg2008]. The  coefficient in  uniqueSVP problems are  according  to  [Reg2003bis].  We  will  list  many  other  problems without defining them: Shortest Vector Problem (SVP), unique Shortest Vector Problem (uniqueSVP), Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP), Closest vector problem (CVP), Learning With Errors (LWE). Also, more assumptions are often made on these problems: particular structure of the lattice (e.g. uniqueSVP rather than SVP), approximate factors etc. 
There is often a trade-off between efficient implementation and security insurance: adding assumptions may  make  the  system  more  vulnerable  but  also  more  realizable  in  practice.  An  important  feature  of lattice-based cryptosystems is that a security proof, when we have one, is based on worst-case hardness rather than average-case hardness.

sources.title: The Security Performance Analysis of Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography – A Case of Cryptocurrency Exchanges - World Scientific Publishing
sources.content:
The Security Performance Analysis of Blockchain System 
Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography | A Case of 
Cryptocurrency Exchanges 
Abel C. H. Chen 
Information & Communications Security Laboratory, 
Chunghwa Telecom Laboratories 
No. 99, Dianyan Road, Yangmei District, Taoyuan 326, Taiwan chchen.scholar@gmail.com 
Accepted 6 September 2025 
Published 26 September 2025 
The current blockchain system for cryptocurrency exchanges primarily employs elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) for generating key pairs in wallets, and elliptic curve digital signature 
algorithms (ECDSA) for generating signatures in transactions. Consequently, with the matu-
ration of quantum computing technology, the current blockchain system faces the risk of 
quantum computing attacks. Quantum computers may potentially counterfeit signatures produced by ECDSA. Therefore, this study analyzes the vulnerabilities of the current blockchain 
system to quantum computing attacks and proposes a post-quantum cryptography (PQC)-
based blockchain system to enhance security by addressing and improving each identi¯ed weakness. Furthermore, this study proposes PQC-based wallets and PQC-based transactions, 
utilizing PQC digital signature algorithms to generate PQC-based signatures for the inputs in 
PQC-based transactions, thereby preventing signatures from being counterfeited by quantum 
computing. Experimental results demonstrate that the e±ciency of the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), a PQC digital signature algorithm, in producing 
wallets, generating signatures, and verifying signatures surpasses that of ECDSA in the current 
blockchain system. Furthermore, the ML-DSA also exhibits a higher security level. 
Keywords: Blockchain; post-quantum cryptography; performance analysis. 
1. Introduction 
In recent years, with the widespread adoption of blockchain systems and technolo-
gies, they have been extensively applied in various ¯elds. The Institute of Electrical 
and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) has furthered this integration by establishing 
multiple standards post-2020. These standards encompass diverse domains, includ-
ing E-commerce transaction evidence collecting (IEEE Standard 3802-2022),1 
This is an Open Access article published by World Scienti¯c Publishing Company. It is distributed under 
the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY) License, which permits use, distribution and 
reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. 
OPEN ACCESS 
Vietnam Journal of Computer Science 
(2025) 1–30 #.c The Author(s) 
DOI: 10.1142/S2196888825500204 
1
electronic contracts (IEEE Standard 3801-2022),2 supply chain ¯nance (IEEE 
Standard 2418.7-2021),3 digital asset management (IEEE Standard 2418.10-2022),4 
E-invoice business (IEEE Standard 2142.1-2021),5 carbon trading applications (IEEE 
Standard 3218-2022),6 cryptocurrency exchanges (IEEE Standard 2140.1-2020),7 
among others. 
While blockchain systems o®er a decentralized architecture and ensure the 
undeniable authenticity and integrity of transactions through cryptographic tech-
niques, the digital signature algorithms (DSAs) in most blockchain systems are still 
based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC).8 However, with the maturation of 
quantum computing technology, ECC faces the risk of being compromised,9 enabling 
attackers with quantum computing capabilities to get ECC private keys and coun-
terfeit legitimate signatures. Consequently, some blockchain systems have begun 
adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC) methods to enhance security, including 
blockchain systems based on lattice-based cryptography10 and hash-based cryp-
tography.11 Additionally, the National Institute of Standards and Technology 
(NIST) in the United States has been soliciting PQC since 2016 and has formulated 
several PQC algorithms, including a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) algorithm 
(i.e. CRYSTALS-Kyber) and DSAs (e.g. CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon, and 
SPHINCS+).12 
In light of enhancing the resistance of blockchain systems against quantum 
computing attacks, this study aims to analyze the cryptographic methods currently 
employed within existing blockchain systems and assess their capability to withstand 
quantum computing attacks. Furthermore, this study endeavors to integrate PQC 
methods, which have been endorsed as standards by the NIST of the United States, 
into blockchain systems, followed by a comparative analysis of system performance. 
The main contributions of this study include: 
. Designing and implementing a blockchain system based on PQC; 
. Verifying and comparing the performance of various PQC standards within 
blockchain systems; 
. Validating and comparing the performance of multiple Proof of Work (PoW) 
parameters within blockchain systems. 
This paper is divided into ¯ve sections. Section 2 discusses the current state of 
blockchain systems and the data structures within blockchain systems, and Sec. 3 
discusses standardization processes of PQC in detail. Section 4 proposes a block-
chain system based on PQC, elaborating on the data structures and providing 
case illustrations. Section 5 experimentally compares the proposed solutions, 
discussing aspects such as e±ciency in wallet generation, e±ciency in signature 
generating, e±ciency in signature veri¯cation, and security analysis of PoW. 
Finally, Sec. 6 concludes the contributions of this study and explores future 
research directions. 
2 A. C. H. Chen
2. The Related Work of Blockchain Systems 
This study primarily draws upon the implementation of a blockchain system by 
Kuznetsov,13 building upon and enhancing its foundational aspects. Section 2.1 
initially elucidates the current state of blockchain systems, delineating the data 
structures of wallets, transactions, blocks, and blockchains, along with the crypto-
graphic techniques employed. Furthermore, Sec. 2.2 discusses the existing PoW 
methods and their security considerations. 
2.1. The data structure of blockchain system 
This subsection introduces the data structures and operational principles of wallets, 
transactions, blocks, and blockchains. 
2.1.1. Wallet 
When generating a wallet, a key pair based on ECC is primarily generated, com-
prising an ECC-based private key and an ECC-based public key, as depicted in 
Fig. 1. Subsequently, during transactions, the ECC-based private key is utilized to 
generate a signature for the transaction content. When other users wish to verify the 
validity of the transaction, they can utilize the ECC-based public key to verify 
the signature. Speci¯cally, the wallet address will be derived from the hash value of 
the ECC-based public key. 
2.1.2. Transaction 
The contents of a transaction mainly comprise the transaction ID, the inputs of the 
transaction, the outputs of the transaction, and the generation time of the trans-
action, as illustrated in Fig. 2. 
The inputs of the transaction refer to the source of the cryptocurrency owned by 
the cryptocurrency holder, which is obtained from previous transactions and may 
stem from multiple past transactions. Therefore, the inputs of the transaction con-
tain multiple inputs, and when transferring cryptocurrency to another user, 
the cryptocurrency holder must use their ECC-based private key to generate an 
ECC-based signature for each input. Each input includes the transaction ID, the 
ECC-based signature, and the ECC-based public key. 
The outputs of the transaction refer to the status of the cryptocurrency for both 
parties after the transfer from one cryptocurrency holder to another. For instance, 
Fig. 1. Wallet. 
The Security Performance Analysis of Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography 3
the outputs of the transaction include the cryptocurrency holder before the trans-
action and the cryptocurrency holder after the transaction, resulting in multiple 
outputs. Each output contains the value and the hash value of the ECC-based public 
key corresponding to the cryptocurrency holder (i.e. the wallet address). 
2.1.3. Block 
In a blockchain system, when conducting transactions, it is necessary to place the 
transactions into a block and generate the blockchain. In this subsection (Sec. 2.1.1), 
we introduce the data structure of a block. Furthermore, in the subsequent 
Fig. 2. Transaction. 
4 A. C. H. Chen
subsection (Sec. 2.1.4), we discuss the blockchain. A block comprises a block hash, 
the previous block hash, a set of transactions, the generation time of the block, and a 
nonce, as depicted in Fig. 3. 
When a transaction occurs, it is added to the \Transactions" ¯eld of a new block, 
and the timestamp of block generation is set. The \Previous Block Hash" ¯eld of this 
new block is then set to the hash value of the preceding block, thus forming the 
blockchain. After setting the values of the aforementioned ¯elds, for the sake of 
integrity veri¯cation, the hash value of the block content is computed. To enhance 
security, a PoW is performed by setting a target di±culty level, denoted as L. The 
hash value obtained after computing the hash of the block content r times is used as 
the block hash. The detailed calculation of the PoW is explained in Sec. 2.2. 
2.1.4. Blockchain 
In a blockchain system, each block stores a block hash and a previous block hash, 
forming the blockchain by pointing to the hash of the previous block. Thus, con-
sidering the ith block as an example, the \Block Hash" ¯eld stores the hash value of 
the ith block, and the \Previous Block Hash" ¯eld stores the hash value of the 
ði 1Þth block, as illustrated in Fig. 4. 
When a user wants to verify the integrity of any block on the blockchain, they can 
obtain the block content and compare the hash value obtained after computing the 
hash of the block content r times with the value in the \Block Hash" ¯eld. If they 
match, it indicates that the content has not been tampered with. Therefore, through 
the blockchain, the integrity of each block on the chain can be con¯rmed, thereby 
establishing the authenticity of the transactions within the block. 
2.2. Proof of work 
To establish block integrity, the process primarily relies on the computation of PoW, 
commonly known as mining, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Assuming the block content is 
Fig. 3. Block. 
The Security Performance Analysis of Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography 5
denoted as b, the hash function is represented by HashðbÞ, and executing the hash 
function r times is denoted as HashrðbÞ, with a target di±culty level denoted as L. 
Initially, the block content b is obtained, and then the hash value HashðbÞ of the 
block content is computed. It is checked whether the ¯rst L bits of the hash value are 
all zeros. If not, the hash value is hashed again until the ¯rst L bits are all zeros. Upon 
termination, the value of r, representing the number of hash function executions, is 
determined, such that HashrðbÞ satis¯es the condition where the ¯rst L bits are all 
zeros. This value of r is then set in the \Nonce" ¯eld. 
2.3. Security issues 
As Shor's quantum algorithm has been proven to factor large integers and solve 
discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time,9 the advancement of quantum 
computing hardware14 is expected to enable cryptanalysis of cryptographic methods 
based on these problems. These methods, collectively referred to as quantum 
vulnerable cryptography (QVC), include RSA and ECC. Consequently, it is neces-
sary to identify and evaluate the use of QVC methods within current blockchain 
systems and to replace them with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) alternatives. 
Fig. 4. Blockchain. 
Fig. 5. Proof of work. 
6 A. C. H. Chen
In blockchain systems, cryptographic applications primarily involve digital 
signatures and hash functions. Since widely adopted platforms such as Bitcoin and 
Ethereum currently rely on the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm 
(ECDSA),15 which is classi¯ed as a QVC method, they lack resistance to quantum 
attacks.16 Therefore, it is essential to replace ECDSA with quantum-resistant digital 
signature schemes, such as the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm 
(ML-DSA)17 or the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA).18 
Regarding hash functions, Bitcoin utilizes Secure Hash Algorithms-2 (SHA-2),19 
while Ethereum uses SHA-3.20 Both SHA-2 and SHA-3 are recognized by NIST as 
secure against quantum cryptanalysis and resistant to collision attacks.21 As such, 
the hash functions employed in these systems are considered to provide su±cient 
security. 
In light of the above, the following sections examine the components within 
blockchain systems that require modi¯cation, speci¯cally addressing the resilience 
against quantum computing attacks with respect to wallets, transactions, blocks, 
and the associated proof-of-work mechanisms in existing blockchain architectures. 
(1) Wallets: Existing blockchain system wallets primarily rely on ECC-based 
private and ECC-based public keys, thus potentially susceptible to quantum 
computing attacks. Consequently, the current blockchain system wallets possess 
quantum-vulnerable weaknesses. 
(2) Transactions: As transactions in existing blockchain systems predominantly 
utilize ECC-based signatures, they too may face vulnerability to quantum 
computing attacks, making them susceptible to counterfeit ECC-based sig-
natures. Thus, transactions in current blockchain systems exhibit weaknesses 
against quantum computing. 
(3) Blocks, Blockchain, Proof of Work: In current blockchain systems, blocks 
and their PoW are constructed based on hash functions (e.g. SHA-256). As 
quantum computing attacks are currently unable to break secure hash algo-
rithms,12 these systems demonstrate resilience against quantum computing. 
Consequently, the primary consideration for PoW lies in the di±culty target 
length, where shorter lengths imply lower security and higher susceptibility 
to successful attacks, while longer lengths entail longer computation times (i.e. 
mining time) and require more computational resources. 
3. The Related Work of Post-Quantum Cryptography 
This section presents a review of related work concerning the standardization process 
and migration timeline of post-quantum cryptography. 
3.1. The standardization process of post-quantum cryptography 
In the third-round report released in September 2022, the NIST has led the evalu-
ation and selection of PQC algorithms for standardization. The evaluation process 
The Security Performance Analysis of Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography 7
has focused on the following three criteria for selecting algorithms as PQC 
standards12: 
(1) Security: The primary and most critical criterion is the ability of an algorithm 
to resist both quantum and classical cryptographic attacks. Algorithms found to 
have security vulnerabilities are eliminated from consideration. 
(3) Cost and Performance: This includes evaluation of computational e±ci-
ency— such as the time required for key pair generation, encryption/decryption, 
and signing/verifying — as well as data size, including key length, ciphertext 
length, and signature size. In particular, for KEMs, which may require ephemeral 
key pair generation in transport layer security protocols and similar applications, 
performance related to key generation and encryption/decryption is emphasized. 
For DSAs, which typically use static key pairs in practical applications, the focus 
is placed on signature generation and veri¯cation times. 
(3) Algorithmic and Implementation Characteristics: This includes °exibi-
lity, simplicity, and ease of integration into existing systems and applications. 
Based on evaluations across the three criteria, lattice-based cryptographic approa-
ches have demonstrated strong security and relatively superior overall e±ciency 
compared to other PQC methods. As a result, lattice-based cryptography has 
emerged as one of the primary directions for post-quantum cryptographic 
standardization. The NIST announced the selection of one KEM algorithm, 
CRYSTALS-Kyber, and three digital signature algorithms  CRYSTALS-
Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS+  as candidates for standardization.12 Subse-
quently, in August 2024, NIST published three Federal Information Processing 
Standards (FIPS) documents: 
(1) FIPS 203 for the KEM standard, titled Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsu-
lation Mechanism (ML-KEM), based on CRYSTALS-Kyber22; 
(2) FIPS 204 for the digital signature standard, titled Module-Lattice-Based 
Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium17; 
(3) FIPS 205 for the digital signature standard, titled Stateless Hash-Based Digital 
Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA), based on SPHINCS+.18 
For KEMs, ML-KEM is lattice-based. To diversify the underlying cryptographic 
foundations, NIST indicated in its fourth-round report (published in March 2025) 
the selection of an additional KEM candidate, HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), which 
is based on code-based cryptography, for standardization.23 For DSAs, both ML-
DSA and Falcon are lattice-based. However, NIST had already selected the hash-
based SPHINCS+ algorithm during the third round and ¯nalized it as the SLH-DSA 
standard, ensuring variety in the cryptographic bases of standardized digital sig-
nature schemes. Table 1 summarizes the current standardized and candidate PQC 
algorithms, categorized by their core cryptographic primitives. The algorithm of 
Falcon, upon standardization, is expected to be o±cially named FN-DSA, short for 
8 A. C. H. Chen
FFT (Fast-Fourier Transform) over NTRU (Nth-degree Truncated polynomial Ring 
Unit)-Lattice-Based DSA. 
Although the Classic McEliece algorithm24 o®ers advantages such as fast 
encryption and decryption speeds25 as well as relatively short ciphertext lengths, it 
su®ers from a relatively long key pair generation time.26 This limitation makes it less 
suitable for applications requiring dynamic generation of ephemeral key pairs.23 As a 
result, in the fourth-round PQC report, the NIST did not select Classic McEliece as a 
candidate for standardization. However, due to its favorable performance char-
acteristics in other aspects, Classic McEliece remains a viable candidate and may be 
considered for standardization by the International Organization for Standardization 
(ISO).23 
3.1.1. The standardization process of additional digital signature schemes 
The currently selected digital signature algorithm standards (i.e. ML-DSA, SLH-
DSA, and FN-DSA) tend to produce relatively large signature sizes, which limits 
their applicability in scenarios requiring short signature lengths. To address this 
limitation, the NIST initiated the evaluation of additional digital signature schemes 
starting in 2023. Following the ¯rst round of evaluation, NIST identi¯ed 14 candi-
date algorithms for advancement to the second round, as outlined in the ¯rst-round 
report of additional digital signature schemes. It is anticipated that this process may

4. The Proposed Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum 
Cryptography 
To enhance the resistance of blockchain systems against quantum computing 
attacks, this study proposes a blockchain system based on PQC, aiming to improve 
security by incorporating PQC methods into the aspects identi¯ed as vulnerable to 
quantum computing attacks in Sec. 2.3. Section 4.1 describes the data structure of 
the proposed blockchain system, while Sec. 4.2 provides case illustrations. 
4.1. The proposed data structure of blockchain system 
This subsection primarily o®ers PQC solutions for wallets and transactions, elabo-
rated in Secs. 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, respectively. Section 4.1.3 describes security con-
siderations and improvement methods for blocks, blockchains, and PoW. To clearly 
illustrate the modi¯cations proposed in this study to the blockchain system, the 
changes are highlighted in red within the architectural diagram, thereby enabling 
readers to better understand the contributions of this work. 
4.1.1. Post-quantum cryptography-based wallet 
The proposed PQC-based wallet mainly consists of a PQC-based private key and a 
PQC-based public key, as illustrated in Fig. 6. When generating a PQC-based wallet, 
a key pair based on PQC is generated, comprising a PQC-based private key and a 
PQC-based public key. Subsequently, during transactions, the PQC-based private 
key can be used to generate a signature for the transaction content. When other users 
wish to verify the validity of the transaction, they can utilize the PQC-based public 
key to verify the signature. Speci¯cally, the wallet address will be derived from the 
hash value of the PQC-based public key.

To prevent signature counterfeiting by quantum computing, the signatures used 
in transactions must be based on PQC. Each transaction input is signed using a

4.1.3. Block, blockchain, and proof of work 
As the blocks, blockchains, and PoW in current blockchain systems possess resilience 
against quantum computing, there is currently no need to modify cryptographic 
algorithms. However, the di±culty target length, denoted as L, will be a primary 
factor to consider. Therefore, in Sec. 5, this study compares the e±ciency of di®erent 
di±culty target lengths. 
Furthermore, considering that the PoW primarily involves computing the hash 
value when the ¯rst L bits are all zeros, this study also explores the probabilities of 
achieving \all zeros" and \all ones" for the ¯rst L bits. While the probabilities of each 
bit being 0 or 1 in the hash value generated by the hash function should ideally follow 
a uniform distribution, in practical computations, these probabilities may not be 
perfectly uniform. Therefore, in Sec. 5.5, this study explores secure PoW algorithms.

5.6. Summary and discussion 
In summary, the experiments conducted in this study provide valuable insights for 
the future deployment of blockchain systems based on PQC. 
(1) The ¯ndings suggest that ML-DSA is a favorable choice for PQC digital signa-
ture. ML-DSA demonstrates superior e±ciency in wallet generation, signature 
generation, and signature veri¯cation compared to the ECDSA currently utilized 
in blockchain systems. Furthermore, ML-DSA exhibits resilience against quan-
tum computing attacks, thereby o®ering a higher level of security compared to 
the ECDSA. 
(2) Falcon algorithm stands out for its e±ciency in signature veri¯cation. Theref-
more, for blockchain systems requiring frequent signature veri¯cation, Falcon 
algorithm is recommended. 
(3) The experiments indicate that the probability of \all L bits of hash values are 
ones" is slightly lower than that of \all L bits of hash values are zeros". There-
fore, it is suggested to enhance security by considering the calculation of \all L 
bits of hash values are ones" in the PoW algorithm.

6. Conclusions and Future Work 
This study analyzes the vulnerabilities of existing blockchain systems to quantum 
computing attacks and proposes a blockchain system based on PQC to address and 
enhance the security of each weakness in current blockchain systems. Speci¯cally, 
this study proposes PQC-based wallets, establishing key pairs based on PQC within 
these wallets. Furthermore, PQC-based transactions are introduced, incorporating 
PQC digital signature algorithms to generate signatures for transaction inputs, thus 
mitigating the risk of signature counterfeiting by quantum computers. Finally, this 
study explores the security of PoW and analyzes the probability distribution of hash 
values, with recommendations and improvements proposed in Sec. 5.6. 
Future research directions may involve the practical deployment of the proposed 
blockchain system based on PQC in commercial cryptocurrency exchange applica-
tions, aiming to enhance the security of existing commercial systems.

Abstract
 The current blockchain system for cryptocurrency exchanges primarily employs elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) for generating key pairs in wallets, and elliptic curve digital signature algorithms (ECDSA) for generating signatures in transactions. Consequently, with the maturation of quantum computing technology, the current blockchain system faces the risk of quantum computing attacks. Quantum computers may potentially counterfeit signatures produced by ECDSA. Therefore, this study analyzes the vulnerabilities of the current blockchain system to quantum computing attacks and proposes a post-quantum cryptography (PQC)-based blockchain system to enhance security by addressing and improving each identified weakness. Furthermore, this study proposes PQC-based wallets and PQC-based transactions, utilizing PQC digital signature algorithms to generate PQC-based signatures for the inputs in PQC-based transactions, thereby preventing signatures from being counterfeited by quantum computing. Experimental results demonstrate that the efficiency of the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), a PQC digital signature algorithm, in producing wallets, generating signatures, and verifying signatures surpasses that of ECDSA in the current blockchain system. Furthermore, the ML-DSA also exhibits a higher security level.
Keywords:Blockchain
post-quantum cryptography
performance analysis
1. Introduction
 In recent years, with the widespread adoption of blockchain systems and technologies, they have been extensively applied in various fields. The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) has furthered this integration by establishing multiple standards post-2020. These standards encompass diverse domains, including E-commerce transaction evidence collecting (IEEE Standard 3802-2022),1 electronic contracts (IEEE Standard 3801-2022),2 supply chain finance (IEEE Standard 2418.7-2021),3 digital asset management (IEEE Standard 2418.10-2022),4 E-invoice business (IEEE Standard 2142.1-2021),5 carbon trading applications (IEEE Standard 3218-2022),6 cryptocurrency exchanges (IEEE Standard 2140.1-2020),7 among others.
 While blockchain systems offer a decentralized architecture and ensure the undeniable authenticity and integrity of transactions through cryptographic techniques, the digital signature algorithms (DSAs) in most blockchain systems are still based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC).8 However, with the maturation of quantum computing technology, ECC faces the risk of being compromised,9 enabling attackers with quantum computing capabilities to get ECC private keys and counterfeit legitimate signatures. Consequently, some blockchain systems have begun adopting post-quantum cryptography (PQC) methods to enhance security, including blockchain systems based on lattice-based cryptography10 and hash-based cryptography.11 Additionally, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in the United States has been soliciting PQC since 2016 and has formulated several PQC algorithms, including a key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) algorithm (i.e. CRYSTALS-Kyber) and DSAs (e.g. CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS+).12
 In light of enhancing the resistance of blockchain systems against quantum computing attacks, this study aims to analyze the cryptographic methods currently employed within existing blockchain systems and assess their capability to withstand quantum computing attacks. Furthermore, this study endeavors to integrate PQC methods, which have been endorsed as standards by the NIST of the United States, into blockchain systems, followed by a comparative analysis of system performance. The main contributions of this study include:
Designing and implementing a blockchain system based on PQC;
Verifying and comparing the performance of various PQC standards within blockchain systems;
Validating and comparing the performance of multiple Proof of Work (PoW) parameters within blockchain systems.
 This paper is divided into five sections. Section 2 discusses the current state of blockchain systems and the data structures within blockchain systems, and Sec. 3 discusses standardization processes of PQC in detail. Section 4 proposes a blockchain system based on PQC, elaborating on the data structures and providing case illustrations. Section 5 experimentally compares the proposed solutions, discussing aspects such as efficiency in wallet generation, efficiency in signature generating, efficiency in signature verification, and security analysis of PoW. Finally, Sec. 6 concludes the contributions of this study and explores future research directions.
2. The Related Work of Blockchain Systems
 This study primarily draws upon the implementation of a blockchain system by Kuznetsov,13 building upon and enhancing its foundational aspects. Section 2.1 initially elucidates the current state of blockchain systems, delineating the data structures of wallets, transactions, blocks, and blockchains, along with the cryptographic techniques employed. Furthermore, Sec. 2.2 discusses the existing PoW methods and their security considerations.
2.1. The data structure of blockchain system
 This subsection introduces the data structures and operational principles of wallets, transactions, blocks, and blockchains.
2.1.1. Wallet
 When generating a wallet, a key pair based on ECC is primarily generated, comprising an ECC-based private key and an ECC-based public key, as depicted in Fig. 1. Subsequently, during transactions, the ECC-based private key is utilized to generate a signature for the transaction content. When other users wish to verify the validity of the transaction, they can utilize the ECC-based public key to verify the signature. Specifically, the wallet address will be derived from the hash value of the ECC-based public key.
Fig. 1.  Wallet.
2.1.2. Transaction
 The contents of a transaction mainly comprise the transaction ID, the inputs of the transaction, the outputs of the transaction, and the generation time of the transaction, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
Fig. 2.  Transaction.
 The inputs of the transaction refer to the source of the cryptocurrency owned by the cryptocurrency holder, which is obtained from previous transactions and may stem from multiple past transactions. Therefore, the inputs of the transaction contain multiple inputs, and when transferring cryptocurrency to another user, the cryptocurrency holder must use their ECC-based private key to generate an ECC-based signature for each input. Each input includes the transaction ID, the ECC-based signature, and the ECC-based public key.
 The outputs of the transaction refer to the status of the cryptocurrency for both parties after the transfer from one cryptocurrency holder to another. For instance, the outputs of the transaction include the cryptocurrency holder before the transaction and the cryptocurrency holder after the transaction, resulting in multiple outputs. Each output contains the value and the hash value of the ECC-based public key corresponding to the cryptocurrency holder (i.e. the wallet address).
2.1.3. Block
 In a blockchain system, when conducting transactions, it is necessary to place the transactions into a block and generate the blockchain. In this subsection (Sec. 2.1.1), we introduce the data structure of a block. Furthermore, in the subsequent subsection (Sec. 2.1.4), we discuss the blockchain. A block comprises a block hash, the previous block hash, a set of transactions, the generation time of the block, and a nonce, as depicted in Fig. 3.
Fig. 3.  Block.
 When a transaction occurs, it is added to the “Transactions” field of a new block, and the timestamp of block generation is set. The “Previous Block Hash” field of this new block is then set to the hash value of the preceding block, thus forming the blockchain. After setting the values of the aforementioned fields, for the sake of integrity verification, the hash value of the block content is computed. To enhance security, a PoW is performed by setting a target difficulty level, denoted as L. The hash value obtained after computing the hash of the block content r times is used as the block hash. The detailed calculation of the PoW is explained in Sec. 2.2.
2.1.4. Blockchain
 In a blockchain system, each block stores a block hash and a previous block hash, forming the blockchain by pointing to the hash of the previous block. Thus, considering the ith block as an example, the “Block Hash” field stores the hash value of the ith block, and the “Previous Block Hash” field stores the hash value of the  ( i − 1 ) th block, as illustrated in Fig. 4.
Fig. 4.  Blockchain.
 When a user wants to verify the integrity of any block on the blockchain, they can obtain the block content and compare the hash value obtained after computing the hash of the block content r times with the value in the “Block Hash” field. If they match, it indicates that the content has not been tampered with. Therefore, through the blockchain, the integrity of each block on the chain can be confirmed, thereby establishing the authenticity of the transactions within the block.
2.2. Proof of work
 To establish block integrity, the process primarily relies on the computation of PoW, commonly known as mining, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Assuming the block content is denoted as b, the hash function is represented by  H a s h ( b ) , and executing the hash function r times is denoted as  H a s h r ( b ) , with a target difficulty level denoted as L. Initially, the block content b is obtained, and then the hash value  H a s h ( b )  of the block content is computed. It is checked whether the first L bits of the hash value are all zeros. If not, the hash value is hashed again until the first L bits are all zeros. Upon termination, the value of r, representing the number of hash function executions, is determined, such that  H a s h r ( b )  satisfies the condition where the first L bits are all zeros. This value of r is then set in the “Nonce” field.
Fig. 5.  Proof of work.
2.3. Security issues
 As Shor’s quantum algorithm has been proven to factor large integers and solve discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time,9 the advancement of quantum computing hardware14 is expected to enable cryptanalysis of cryptographic methods based on these problems. These methods, collectively referred to as quantum vulnerable cryptography (QVC), include RSA and ECC. Consequently, it is necessary to identify and evaluate the use of QVC methods within current blockchain systems and to replace them with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) alternatives.
 In blockchain systems, cryptographic applications primarily involve digital signatures and hash functions. Since widely adopted platforms such as Bitcoin and Ethereum currently rely on the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA),15 which is classified as a QVC method, they lack resistance to quantum attacks.16 Therefore, it is essential to replace ECDSA with quantum-resistant digital signature schemes, such as the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA)17 or the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA).18 Regarding hash functions, Bitcoin utilizes Secure Hash Algorithms-2 (SHA-2),19 while Ethereum uses SHA-3.20 Both SHA-2 and SHA-3 are recognized by NIST as secure against quantum cryptanalysis and resistant to collision attacks.21 As such, the hash functions employed in these systems are considered to provide sufficient security.
 In light of the above, the following sections examine the components within blockchain systems that require modification, specifically addressing the resilience against quantum computing attacks with respect to wallets, transactions, blocks, and the associated proof-of-work mechanisms in existing blockchain architectures.
(1)
Wallets: Existing blockchain system wallets primarily rely on ECC-based private and ECC-based public keys, thus potentially susceptible to quantum computing attacks. Consequently, the current blockchain system wallets possess quantum-vulnerable weaknesses.
(2)
Transactions: As transactions in existing blockchain systems predominantly utilize ECC-based signatures, they too may face vulnerability to quantum computing attacks, making them susceptible to counterfeit ECC-based signatures. Thus, transactions in current blockchain systems exhibit weaknesses against quantum computing.
(3)
Blocks, Blockchain, Proof of Work: In current blockchain systems, blocks and their PoW are constructed based on hash functions (e.g. SHA-256). As quantum computing attacks are currently unable to break secure hash algorithms,12 these systems demonstrate resilience against quantum computing. Consequently, the primary consideration for PoW lies in the difficulty target length, where shorter lengths imply lower security and higher susceptibility to successful attacks, while longer lengths entail longer computation times (i.e. mining time) and require more computational resources.
3. The Related Work of Post-Quantum Cryptography
 This section presents a review of related work concerning the standardization process and migration timeline of post-quantum cryptography.
3.1. The standardization process of post-quantum cryptography
 In the third-round report released in September 2022, the NIST has led the evaluation and selection of PQC algorithms for standardization. The evaluation process has focused on the following three criteria for selecting algorithms as PQC standards12:
(1)
Security: The primary and most critical criterion is the ability of an algorithm to resist both quantum and classical cryptographic attacks. Algorithms found to have security vulnerabilities are eliminated from consideration.
(3)
Cost and Performance: This includes evaluation of computational efficiency — such as the time required for key pair generation, encryption/decryption, and signing/verifying — as well as data size, including key length, ciphertext length, and signature size. In particular, for KEMs, which may require ephemeral key pair generation in transport layer security protocols and similar applications, performance related to key generation and encryption/decryption is emphasized. For DSAs, which typically use static key pairs in practical applications, the focus is placed on signature generation and verification times.
(3)
Algorithmic and Implementation Characteristics: This includes flexibility, simplicity, and ease of integration into existing systems and applications.
 Based on evaluations across the three criteria, lattice-based cryptographic approaches have demonstrated strong security and relatively superior overall efficiency compared to other PQC methods. As a result, lattice-based cryptography has emerged as one of the primary directions for post-quantum cryptographic standardization. The NIST announced the selection of one KEM algorithm, CRYSTALS-Kyber, and three digital signature algorithms — CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon, and SPHINCS+ — as candidates for standardization.12 Subsequently, in August 2024, NIST published three Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) documents:
(1)
FIPS 203 for the KEM standard, titled Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), based on CRYSTALS-Kyber22;
(2)
FIPS 204 for the digital signature standard, titled Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), based on CRYSTALS-Dilithium17;
(3)
FIPS 205 for the digital signature standard, titled Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA), based on SPHINCS+.18
 For KEMs, ML-KEM is lattice-based. To diversify the underlying cryptographic foundations, NIST indicated in its fourth-round report (published in March 2025) the selection of an additional KEM candidate, HQC (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic), which is based on code-based cryptography, for standardization.23 For DSAs, both ML-DSA and Falcon are lattice-based. However, NIST had already selected the hash-based SPHINCS+ algorithm during the third round and finalized it as the SLH-DSA standard, ensuring variety in the cryptographic bases of standardized digital signature schemes. Table 1 summarizes the current standardized and candidate PQC algorithms, categorized by their core cryptographic primitives. The algorithm of Falcon, upon standardization, is expected to be officially named FN-DSA, short for FFT (Fast-Fourier Transform) over NTRU (Nth-degree Truncated polynomial Ring Unit)-Lattice-Based DSA.

 Although the Classic McEliece algorithm24 offers advantages such as fast encryption and decryption speeds25 as well as relatively short ciphertext lengths, it suffers from a relatively long key pair generation time.26 This limitation makes it less suitable for applications requiring dynamic generation of ephemeral key pairs.23 As a result, in the fourth-round PQC report, the NIST did not select Classic McEliece as a candidate for standardization. However, due to its favorable performance characteristics in other aspects, Classic McEliece remains a viable candidate and may be considered for standardization by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO).23
3.1.1. The standardization process of additional digital signature schemes
 The currently selected digital signature algorithm standards (i.e. ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and FN-DSA) tend to produce relatively large signature sizes, which limits their applicability in scenarios requiring short signature lengths. To address this limitation, the NIST initiated the evaluation of additional digital signature schemes starting in 2023. Following the first round of evaluation, NIST identified 14 candidate algorithms for advancement to the second round, as outlined in the first-round report of additional digital signature schemes. It is anticipated that this process may ultimately lead to the selection of an additional digital signature standard featuring shorter signature lengths and faster signing performance.27
3.2. The migration timeline of post-quantum cryptography
 In response to the ongoing advancements in quantum computing hardware and quantum algorithm technologies, the NIST released a draft roadmap in November 2024 outlining the transition to PQC standards. This draft explicitly specifies the planned deprecation and eventual prohibition timelines for cryptographic schemes based on RSA and ECC.28

Among elliptic curve schemes, Curve P-224 corresponds to 112-bit security, and Curve P-256 to 128-bit security.29

3.3. Discussions
 As NIST has conducted a global call for PQC algorithm submissions and selected those with strong security and high performance for standardization as U.S. federal government standards, it is anticipated that future global development and implementation efforts will align with these selected algorithms. While other high-quality algorithms may not be included in the standardized list, this study focuses solely on those chosen as U.S. federal standards, taking into account anticipated industry adoption trends.
 Furthermore, in blockchain system applications, the primary cryptographic functions involve DSAs and hash functions, with limited use of KEMs. More specifically, KEMs are typically associated with protocols like Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol,30 whereas blockchain systems are expected to rely more heavily on digital signatures and hashing. In light of this, this study concentrates on DSAs and hash functions, without an in-depth discussion of KEMs. Additionally, it is noted that in blockchain wallet generation, the computation time for key pair generation is typically a one-time cost. The ongoing computational focus lies in the signing and verification processes. Therefore, the computation times of signature generation and signature verification are of greater relevance for performance evaluation in such applications.
4. The Proposed Blockchain System Based on Post-Quantum Cryptography
 To enhance the resistance of blockchain systems against quantum computing attacks, this study proposes a blockchain system based on PQC, aiming to improve security by incorporating PQC methods into the aspects identified as vulnerable to quantum computing attacks in Sec. 2.3. Section 4.1 describes the data structure of the proposed blockchain system, while Sec. 4.2 provides case illustrations.
4.1. The proposed data structure of blockchain system
 This subsection primarily offers PQC solutions for wallets and transactions, elaborated in Secs. 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, respectively. Section 4.1.3 describes security considerations and improvement methods for blocks, blockchains, and PoW. To clearly illustrate the modifications proposed in this study to the blockchain system, the changes are highlighted in red within the architectural diagram, thereby enabling readers to better understand the contributions of this work.
4.1.1. Post-quantum cryptography-based wallet
 The proposed PQC-based wallet mainly consists of a PQC-based private key and a PQC-based public key, as illustrated in Fig. 6. When generating a PQC-based wallet, a key pair based on PQC is generated, comprising a PQC-based private key and a PQC-based public key. Subsequently, during transactions, the PQC-based private key can be used to generate a signature for the transaction content. When other users wish to verify the validity of the transaction, they can utilize the PQC-based public key to verify the signature. Specifically, the wallet address will be derived from the hash value of the PQC-based public key.
Fig. 6.  PQC-based wallet.
4.1.2. Post-quantum cryptography-based transaction
 Figure 7 depicts the data structure of PQC-based transactions proposed in this study. It primarily comprises a PQC-based signature and a PQC-based public key, detailed as follows.
Fig. 7.  PQC-based transaction.
 To prevent signature counterfeiting by quantum computing, the signatures used in transactions must be based on PQC. Each transaction input is signed using a PQC-based signature generated by the PQC-based private key in the PQC-based wallet. Furthermore, the corresponding PQC-based public key is stored alongside each transaction input. In the transaction outputs, the modification is made accordingly, as the wallet address in the PQC-based wallet is already the hash value of the PQC-based public key.
4.1.3. Block, blockchain, and proof of work
 As the blocks, blockchains, and PoW in current blockchain systems possess resilience against quantum computing, there is currently no need to modify cryptographic algorithms. However, the difficulty target length, denoted as L, will be a primary factor to consider. Therefore, in Sec. 5, this study compares the efficiency of different difficulty target lengths.
 Furthermore, considering that the PoW primarily involves computing the hash value when the first L bits are all zeros, this study also explores the probabilities of achieving “all zeros” and “all ones” for the first L bits. While the probabilities of each bit being 0 or 1 in the hash value generated by the hash function should ideally follow a uniform distribution, in practical computations, these probabilities may not be perfectly uniform. Therefore, in Sec. 5.5, this study explores secure PoW algorithms.

 This subsection provides a case study illustrating the blockchain system proposed in this study, demonstrating the operation process of PQC-based wallets, PQC-based transactions, blocks, and blockchains.

 In the scenario, suppose there are four users (namely Alice, Bob, Cara, and David) conducting cryptocurrency exchanges. (2)
 Cara has acquired 7 units of cryptocurrency in the transaction with Transaction ID  t c , and Cara’s balance is only 7 units.
(3)
 Both Bob and David have a balance of 0 units of cryptocurrency.
Transaction Scenarios:
(1)
 Transaction ID  t j : Alice transfers 5 units of cryptocurrency to Bob.
(2)
 Transaction ID  t j + 1 : Cara transfers 7 units of cryptocurrency to Bob.
(3)
 Transaction ID  t j + 2 : Bob transfers 12 units of cryptocurrency to David.

 The PQC-based transactions generated in the transaction scenarios of the case study are explained as follows:
 (1) Transaction ID  t j  (Alice transfers 5 units of cryptocurrency to Bob):
 Since Alice has acquired 5 units of cryptocurrency in the transaction with Transaction ID  t a , she can transfer the 5 units to Bob using the cryptocurrency obtained in Transaction  t a . Therefore, to create the transaction with Transaction ID  t j , a single input is set in the transaction input field, where the “Transaction ID” field is  t a . In the “PQC-based Signature” field of this input, Alice’s signature signed by her PQC-based private key is stored to confirm that the transaction is indeed conducted by Alice.  Regarding the outputs, as it primarily affects Alice’s and Bob’s wallets, the transaction outputs include 2 entries. In the second output entry, the “PQC-based Public Key Hash” field represents Bob’s wallet address, and the “Amount” field is 5, indicating that Bob receives 5 units in his wallet after this transaction.

 Since Cara has acquired 7 units of cryptocurrency in the transaction with Transaction ID  t c , she can transfer the 7 units to Bob using the cryptocurrency obtained in Transaction  t c . Therefore, to create the transaction with Transaction  t j + 1 , a single input is set in the transaction input field, where the “Transaction ID” field is  t c . In the “PQC-based Signature” field of this input, Cara’s signature signed by her PQC-based private key is stored to confirm that the transaction is indeed conducted by Cara. Furthermore, Cara’s PQC-based public key is stored in the “PQC-based Public Key” field for subsequent signature verification.
 Regarding the outputs, as it primarily affects Cara’s and Bob’s wallets, the transaction outputs include 2 entries. In the first output entry, the “PQC-based Public Key Hash” field represents Cara’s wallet address, and the “Amount” field is 0, indicating that Cara’s wallet balance is 0 units after this transaction. In the second output entry, the “PQC-based Public Key Hash” field represents Bob’s wallet address, and the “Amount” field is 7, indicating that Bob receives 7 units in his wallet after this transaction.
 (3) Transaction ID  t j + 2  (Bob transfers 12 units of cryptocurrency to David):
 As Bob transfers 12 units of cryptocurrency to David, and Bob does not have a single transaction record of receiving more than 12 units, Bob needs to combine multiple transactions (i.e. Transaction  t j  and Transaction  t j + 1 ) to have 12 units available for transfer to David. To create the transaction with Transaction  t j + 2 , multiple inputs are included in the transaction input. In the first input, the “Transaction ID” field is  t j , and Bob’s signature signed by his PQC-based private key is stored in the “PQC-based Signature” field to confirm that the transaction is indeed conducted by Bob. Furthermore, Bob’s PQC-based public key is stored in the “PQC-based Public Key” field for subsequent signature verification. In the second input, the “Transaction ID” field is  t j + 1 , and similar to the first input, another Bob’s signature signed by his PQC-based private key is generated, and respective PQC-based signatures and public keys are stored.
 Regarding the outputs, as it primarily affects Bob’s and David’s wallets, the transaction outputs include 2 entries. In the first output entry, the “PQC-based Public Key Hash” field represents Bob’s wallet address, and the “Amount” field is 0, indicating that Bob’s wallet balance is 0 units after this transaction. In the second output entry, the “PQC-based Public Key Hash” field represents David’s wallet address, and the “Amount” field is 12, indicating that David receives 12 units in his wallet after this transaction.
 Explanation of the quantum-based blockchain generated from the transaction scenarios in the case study is as follows:
 (1) Block i (Alice transfers 5 units of cryptocurrency to Bob):
 When the transaction with Transaction ID  t j  occurs, Block i is generated to verify the integrity of Transaction  t j . In the “Previous Block Hash” field of Block i, the hash of Block  ( i − 1 )  is stored, pointing to the previous block and forming the blockchain. In the “Transactions” field, Transaction  t j  is stored, and the “Generation Time” field is set to the time when the block was produced. Subsequently, based on the PoW algorithm, the block hash and nonce  r i  are generated from the block content.

In the “Transactions” field, Transaction  t j + 1  is stored, and the “Generation Time” field is set to the time when the block was produced. Subsequently, appropriate values for the “Block Hash” and “Nonce” fields are generated according to the PoW algorithm.
 (3) Block  ( i + 2 )  (Bob transfers 12 units of cryptocurrency to David):
